exampleAnswers.title: Calculating Improper Integrals With an Unbounded Upper Limit

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

\begin{align} \int_1^\infty \dfrac {3}{\sqrt{x^5}} \,\textrm{d}x &= \lim_{a \to \infty} \int_1^a \dfrac {3}{\sqrt{x^5}} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = 3 \lim_{a \to \infty} \int_1^a x^{-5/2} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = 3\lim_{a \to \infty}\left[ -\dfrac{2}{3}x^{-3/2} \right ]_1^a \\[5pt] & = -2 \cdot \lim_{a \to \infty}\left[ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^3}} \right ]_1^a \\[5pt] &= -2 \cdot \lim_{a \to \infty} \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a^3}} - \dfrac {1}{\sqrt{1^3}}\right) \\[5pt] &= -2 \left (0 - 1\right) \\[5pt] &=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{ 2}. \end{align}

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

\begin{align} \int_1^\infty \dfrac {12}{\sqrt[3]{s^7}} \,\textrm{d}s &= \lim_{a \to \infty} \int_1^a \dfrac {12}{\sqrt[3]{s^7}} \,\textrm{d}s\\[5pt] & = 12 \lim_{a \to \infty} \int_1^a s^{-7/3} \,\textrm{d}s\\[5pt] & = 12\lim_{a \to \infty}\left[ -\dfrac{3}{4}s^{-4/3} \right ]_1^a \\[5pt] & = -9 \cdot \lim_{a \to \infty}\left[ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt[3]{s^4}} \right ]_1^a \\[5pt] &= -9 \cdot \lim_{a \to \infty} \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt[3]{a^4}} - \dfrac {1}{\sqrt[3]{1^4}}\right) \\[5pt] &= -9 \left (0 - 1\right) \\[5pt] &=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{ 9}. \end{align}

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating Improper Integrals With an Unbounded Upper Limit Using Substitution

question.explanation:
First, we substitute $u=2x+4.$ Differentiating, we get

\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{1}{2}\,\textrm{d}u =\textrm{d}x. \]

Since $u \to \infty$ when $x \to \infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=2x+4$ is as follows:

$x$ $0$ $\infty$
$u$ $4$ $\infty$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

\begin{align*} \int_0^\infty \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{(2x+4)^3}} \,\textrm{d}x &= \int_4^\infty \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{u^3}} \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\,\textrm{d}u \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2}\int_4^\infty \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{u^3}} \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Finally, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

\begin{align*} \displaystyle \int_0^\infty \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{(2x+4)^3}} \,\textrm{d}x &=\dfrac{3}{2}\int_4^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{u^3}} \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{3}{2}\int_4^{\infty} u^{-{3}/{2}} \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{3}{2}\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \int_4^a u^{-{3}/{2}} \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{3}{2}\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[-2 u^{-{1}/{2}}\right]_4^a \\[5pt] &=-3 \cdot \lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\right]_4^a \\[5pt] &=-3\cdot\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a}}-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{4}} \right]\\[5pt] &=-3\cdot \left( 0 -\dfrac 1 2 \right)\\[5pt] &=\frac{3}{2}. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating Improper Integrals With an Unbounded Upper Limit Using Substitution

question.explanation:
First, we substitute $u=1+x^3.$ Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 3x^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{1}{3}\textrm{d}u =x^2\,\textrm{d}x. \]

Since $ u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=1+x^3$ is as follows:

$x$ $0$ $\infty$
$u$ $1$ $\infty$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

\begin{align} \displaystyle \int_0^\infty \dfrac{x^2}{\left(1+x^3\right)^4} \,\textrm{d}x &=\dfrac{1}{3}\int_1^\infty \dfrac{1}{u^4} \,\textrm{d}u. \end{align}

Finally, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

\begin{align*} \displaystyle \int_0^\infty \dfrac{x^2}{\left(1+x^3\right)^4} \,\textrm{d}x &=\dfrac{1}{3}\int_1^\infty \dfrac{1}{u^4} \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3}\int_1^\infty u^{-4} \,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3}\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \int_1^a u^{-4} \,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] %&=\dfrac{1}{3}\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \int_1^a \left[-\dfrac{1}{3}u^{-3} \,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3}\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[ -\dfrac{1}{3}u^{-3} \right]_1^a\\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{9} \lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[ \dfrac{1}{u^3}\right]_1^a\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{1}{9}\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left(\dfrac{1}{a^3} - 1 \right)\\[5pt] &= - \dfrac{1}{9}\left(0 - 1\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{9}. \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating Improper Integrals With an Unbounded Lower Limit

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to-\infty.$

\begin{align*} \int_{-\infty}^{-1} \dfrac{10}{x^6} \,\textrm{d}x & =10\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \int_a^{-1} x^{-6} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=10\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ -\dfrac{1}{5}x^{-5} \right]_a^{-1}\\[5pt] &=-2\cdot\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ \dfrac{1}{x^5} \right]_a^{-1}\\[5pt] &=-2\cdot\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ \dfrac{1}{(-1)^5}- \dfrac{1}{a^5} \right]\\[5pt] &=-2\cdot\left(-1-0\right)\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{2}. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating Improper Integrals With an Unbounded Lower Limit

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
First, we substitute $u=x^3-1.$ Differentiating, we get

\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 3x^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}u =3x^2\textrm{d}x. \]

Since $u \to -\infty$ when $x \to -\infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x^3-1$ is as follows:

$x$ $-\infty$ $-2$
$u$ $-\infty$ $-9$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

\[ \int_{-\infty}^{-2} \dfrac{6x^2}{(x^3-1)^3} \,\textrm{d}x = \int_{-\infty}^{-9} \dfrac{2}{u^3} \,\textrm{d}u \]

Finally, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to-\infty.$

\begin{align*} \int_{-\infty}^{-9} \dfrac{2}{u^3} \,\textrm{d}u & =2\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \int_a^{-9} u^{-3} \,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=2\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ -\dfrac{1}{2}u^{-2} \right]_a^{-9}\\[5pt] &=-1\cdot\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ \dfrac{1}{u^2} \right]_a^{-9}\\[5pt] &=-1\cdot\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ \dfrac{1}{(-9)^2}- \dfrac{1}{a^2} \right]\\[5pt] &=-1\cdot\left(\dfrac{1}{81}-0\right)\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-\dfrac{1}{81}}. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating Improper Integrals With an Unbounded Lower Limit

question.explanation:
We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

\begin{align*} \displaystyle \int_1^\infty \dfrac{1}{2-3z} \,\textrm{d}z &=\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \int_1^a \dfrac{1}{2-3z} \,\textrm{d}z\\[5pt] &=\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[ -\dfrac13 \cdot \ln|2-3z| \right]_1^a\\[5pt] &= -\dfrac13 \cdot\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \big[ \ln|2-3z| \big]_1^a\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac13 \cdot\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left( \ln|2-3a| -\ln|-1| \right)\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac13 \cdot \lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left( \ln|2-3a| \right)\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac13 \cdot \left( \infty \right)\\[5pt] &=-\infty. \end{align*} Therefore, the integral is divergent.

We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty.$

\[ \eqalign{ \int_{-\infty}^{-1} \dfrac {\textrm{d}t}{\sqrt{2-3t}} & = \lim_{a \to -\infty} \int_{a}^{-1} \dfrac {\textrm{d}t}{\sqrt{2-3t}}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{a \to -\infty} \left[-\dfrac 23 \sqrt{2-3t} \right]_{a}^{-1} \\[5pt] &=-\dfrac 23\cdot\lim_{a \to -\infty}\left(\sqrt{2+3}-\sqrt{2-3a} \right)\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac {2\sqrt 5}3+\dfrac 23 \lim_{a \to -\infty}\sqrt{2-3a}\\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{2\sqrt 5}{3}+\infty\\[5pt] &=\infty. } \]

Therefore, the integral is divergent.

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

\[ \eqalign{ \int_0^\infty \dfrac {2}{\sqrt[3]{2z+1}} \,\textrm{d}z & = \lim_{a \to \infty} \int_0^a\dfrac {2}{\sqrt[3]{2z+1}} \,\textrm{d}z\\[5pt] & = \lim_{a \to \infty}\left[\dfrac { 3}{2} (2z+1)^{2/ 3} \right]_0^a \\[5pt] & = \dfrac32\cdot\lim_{a \to \infty}\left[ (2z+1)^{2/ 3} \right]_0^a \\[5pt] &=\dfrac32\cdot\lim_{a \to \infty} \left( (2a+1)^{2/ 3} -1\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac32\cdot\infty\\[5pt] &=\infty. } \] Therefore, the integral is divergent.

We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty.$

\[ \eqalign{ \int_{-\infty}^0 \dfrac {\textrm{d}z}{\sqrt{1-z}} & = \lim_{a \to -\infty} \int_{a}^0 \dfrac {\textrm{d}z}{\sqrt{1-z}}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{a \to -\infty} \left[-2\sqrt{1-z} \right]_{a}^0 \\[5pt] &=-2\cdot\lim_{a \to -\infty}\left(\sqrt{1-0}-\sqrt{1-a} \right)\\[5pt] &=-2+2\cdot\lim_{a \to -\infty}\sqrt{1-a}\\[5pt] &= -2+2\cdot\infty\\[5pt] &=\infty. } \]

Therefore, the integral is divergent.
